title: Nakhon Sawan Temple & Shrine Plan: 2 Days in Paknampho
metaDesc: A full 2-day Nakhon Sawan temple-and-shrine itinerary in Thailand: pray at the Chao Pho Thepharak-Chao Mae Thapthim shrine, Wat Khiri Wong, Wat Woranat Banphot and Wat Nakhon Sawan, plus the old Chinese quarter of Paknampho, planned day by day.
keywords: Nakhon Sawan temples, Paknampho shrines, Nakhon Sawan temple tour, Paknampho Chinese town, Wat Khiri Wong
h1:
Nakhon Sawan Temple & Shrine Plan
Praying Through the Chinese Town of Paknampho
intro: Nakhon Sawan, which locals simply call "Paknampho," is a town where Chinese culture has soaked into every lane, from riverside shrines more than a century old to hilltop temples that look out over the headwaters of the Chao Phraya. We've laid out a faith-and-merit route that fits neatly into 2 days, so you can pray for good fortune and still see the everyday life of an overseas-Chinese community that's genuinely still breathing here.

blocks.html: If you're after a town where Chinese and Thai life blend together seamlessly, Nakhon Sawan is one of them. Overseas Chinese settled at Paknampho, the point where the Ping and Nan rivers meet to form the headwaters of the Chao Phraya, generations ago, and they left their mark everywhere: shrines, an old market, the food, and the deity processions that are now listed as part of the country's intangible cultural heritage. On this trip we string Thai temples and Chinese shrines into a single route, walked at an easy pace over 2 days with no rush.

Day one covers the town and the riverside, focusing on the Chinese shrines and the in-town temples that are easy to walk between. Day two heads up the hills to pray and take in the views, finishing at the source of the Chao Phraya River. Everything sits in and around the Mueang district, just a few minutes' drive or ride between stops, which makes it work whether you've come specifically for this or you're just breaking up a trip heading north.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Chinese shrines, in-town temples & Paknampho market

items.activity: Start at the Chao Pho Thepharak-Chao Mae Thapthim shrine (Chao Pho Khwae Yai shrine)
items.note: A riverside shrine on the Chao Phraya, across from Paknampho market and more than 130 years old. Inside you'll find Pung Thao Kong, the deity Guan Yu, and Chao Mae Thapthim. Nakhon Sawan locals treat it as the town's main shrine. Come early before the crowds and you can get some lovely shots of the red Chinese architecture.

items.activity: Walk Paknampho market & the old quarter
items.note: The old market across from the shrine is a Chinese quarter that's still very much alive, with shops selling dried goods, Chinese medicine, sweets, and Chinese-style breakfast fare. It's a pleasant stroll past the old shophouses.

items.activity: Pray at Wat Nakhon Sawan, a royal temple
items.note: On Kosi Road in the town centre, this old temple comes with a story that an Ayutthaya-era king once stopped to pay his respects. It's a paired "two siblings" temple, shaded and calm in the middle of town, and easy to visit straight after the market.
This area is the home of pak mo (steamed rice-sheet) noodles, mochi, and old-school Chinese cooking. Just pick a spot in the market or along Kosi Road.
A temple on a low hill within the town, open 06:00-18:00. It has an old ordination hall and views over the town, making it a good afternoon stop that stays quiet.

items.activity: Stroll the Chao Phraya riverside, watch the sunset
items.note: Close out day one by the river in town. The evening breeze is pleasant and you'll see Paknampho life along the water.

blocks.title: What to wear
blocks.html: Both temples and shrines are sacred places, so a sleeved top and trousers or a skirt that covers the knees is more respectful and more comfortable. Chinese shrines usually sell incense and offerings out front, so keep some small cash notes on you.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Hilltop temples, city views & the Chao Phraya headwaters

items.activity: Climb to Wat Khiri Wong, pray at the Chulamani Chedi
items.note: A temple on Dao Dueng hill within the town, where the golden Chulamani Chedi sits gleaming on the summit. Climb up onto the chedi's base and you can see the whole of Nakhon Sawan, including Khao Kop, Bueng Boraphet, and the source of the Chao Phraya. Inside there are statues of famous monks such as Somdej To, Luang Pu Thuat and Luang Pho Sot. Go early while the air is still cool.

An old temple on Khao Kop hill with a chedi and a Buddha footprint, a town hill that's visible from many angles. Head up to pray and you'll get a view of the other side of town. Nearby there's a cliffside goddess shrine worth a stop.
Head back into town to eat. The Paknampho area has noodles, chicken or duck over rice, and Chinese desserts to choose from.

items.activity: Pasan, symbol of the Chao Phraya's source
items.note: An architectural landmark right where the Ping and Nan rivers merge into the Chao Phraya, and a popular check-in and photo spot. You can stroll along the river and get the full picture of why this town is called Paknampho ("river mouth").

items.activity: Stop by the shrine & grab gifts before heading home
items.note: If you haven't prayed everywhere, loop back to the Chao Pho Thepharak shrine for one more round of blessings, then pick up Paknampho mochi and Chinese sweets to take home.

blocks.html: Paknampho is where overseas Chinese came ashore and settled along the river long ago, so Chinese culture runs deeper here than the shop signs suggest. The Chao Pho Thepharak-Chao Mae Thapthim shrine is the spiritual heart of the town's Chinese community, and the event that put Nakhon Sawan on the national map is the Paknampho deity procession during Chinese New Year, with its golden dragon, lion, and Eng Gor parades that have run continuously for more than a hundred years.

items: The riverside shrine — the Chao Pho Thepharak-Chao Mae Thapthim shrine is the heart of the Chinese quarter, set right across from the old market.
Paknampho market — an old trading quarter that still sells dried goods, Chinese medicine, and Chinese-style food every day.
Chinese New Year tradition — the Paknampho deity procession, held every Chinese New Year, is now listed as intangible cultural heritage.
Original Chinese food — pak mo noodles and Paknampho mochi are the town's signature dishes, rooted in the Chinese community.

blocks.text: Key temples & shrines not to skip

items.name: Chao Pho Thepharak-Chao Mae Thapthim shrine
items.blurb: A Chinese shrine on the Chao Phraya River, more than 130 years old and across from Paknampho market. It enshrines Pung Thao Kong, the deity Guan Yu, and Chao Mae Thapthim, and is the main shrine of the town's Chinese community and the starting point of the Chinese New Year deity procession.
items.meta: Mueang district · riverside, across from Paknampho market

items.name: Wat Khiri Wong
items.blurb: A temple on Dao Dueng hill with the golden Chulamani Chedi on the summit. Climb up to pray and you get a view over the whole of Nakhon Sawan, taking in Khao Kop, Bueng Boraphet, and the source of the Chao Phraya. Inside are statues of several famous monks.
items.meta: Mueang district · on Dao Dueng hill

items.name: Wat Woranat Banphot (Khao Kop)
items.blurb: An old temple on Khao Kop hill in the middle of town, with a chedi and a Buddha footprint. Head up to pray for a different view of the town, and nearby there's a cliffside goddess shrine to visit next.
items.meta: Mueang district · on Khao Kop hill

items.name: Wat Nakhon Sawan, a royal temple
items.blurb: An old royal temple in the town centre on Kosi Road, with a story that an Ayutthaya-era king once stopped to pay his respects. It's a paired "two siblings" temple and an easy walk on from Paknampho market.

items.name: Wat Chom Khiri Nak Phrot
items.blurb: A temple on a rise within the town with an old ordination hall and views over the town, open 06:00-18:00. It's a quieter praying spot, good for an afternoon stop.

blocks.title: If you come during Chinese New Year
blocks.html: Late January to early February is the Paknampho deity procession, when the town gets very lively with golden dragon and lion parades and the whole quarter is decorated. If you're set on coming then, book your accommodation several weeks ahead, because rooms fill fast and prices rise. Confirm the exact dates with the municipality's page or the TAT Nakhon Sawan office before you travel.

Most stops are in and around the Mueang district, close together. Driving yourself is the most convenient, since hilltop temples like Khiri Wong and Khao Kop need you to drive up the slope. If you don't have a car, you can call a ride through an app or use a motorbike taxi in town. The shrine and Paknampho market are an easy walk apart, and Pasan is also riverside in the town centre.

items.name: Drive yourself
items.blurb: The most flexible option, easy for getting up to the hilltop temples, with enough parking at the temples and shrines.

items.name: Ride-hail / motorbike taxi
items.blurb: Good if you're only touring in town. Short distances and not pricey.

items.name: Walk
items.blurb: The shrine, Paknampho market and the riverside all link up within comfortable walking distance.

faq.q: How many days do I need to cover the temples and shrines of Nakhon Sawan?
faq.a: The main route, covering the Chinese shrines, the in-town temples and the hilltop temples, fits nicely into 2 days. Day one covers the town and the riverside, day two heads up the hills to pray and take in the views. If you only have one day, focus on the Chao Pho Thepharak shrine, Paknampho market, and Wat Khiri Wong.

faq.q: Where is the Chao Pho Thepharak-Chao Mae Thapthim shrine?
faq.a: It's on the Chao Phraya River in the Mueang district, right across from Paknampho market. It's an old Chinese shrine more than 130 years old and the spiritual heart of the town's Chinese community.

faq.q: Which temple in Nakhon Sawan has views over the town?
faq.a: Wat Khiri Wong on Dao Dueng hill is the best for city views. Climb onto the base of the Chulamani Chedi and you can see the whole town, including Khao Kop, Bueng Boraphet, and the source of the Chao Phraya. Another option is Wat Woranat Banphot on Khao Kop hill, which gives you a different angle on the town.

faq.q: What time of year is the town liveliest?
faq.a: Chinese New Year, from late January to early February, is the Paknampho deity procession, with golden dragon and lion parades and the whole quarter decorated. If you come then, book your accommodation several weeks ahead.

faq.q: How should I dress to visit the temples and shrines?
faq.a: Dress modestly: a sleeved top and trousers or a knee-length skirt. Both temples and shrines are sacred places. Chinese shrines sell incense and offerings out front, so it helps to keep some small cash notes on you.
